subtopic_detail: adjusting an established thyroxine dose at the moment pregnancy is confirmed in a woman with treated hypothyroidism
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 31-year-old woman who has just had a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and she has not yet had a dating scan or any antenatal bloods.

She has taken thyroxine 100 micrograms daily for eight years for autoimmune hypothyroidism and her most recent thyroid function tests, done three months ago as part of routine annual review, showed a thyroid stimulating hormone of 2.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) with a normal free thyroxine. She takes the tablet first thing each morning and has never missed a dose. She is otherwise well, takes a pregnancy multivitamin containing iodine, and asks whether anything about her tablets needs to change now.

data_table.Examination: No goitre, no tremor, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) with normal free thyroxine, taken three months ago
data_table.Medications: Thyroxine 100 micrograms orally each morning, pregnancy multivitamin containing iodine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about her thyroxine today?

options.text: Continue the current dose and add potassium iodide 150 micrograms daily as a separate tablet
options.rationale: Additional iodine is not a substitute for adequate thyroxine in a woman whose gland has already failed, and her pregnancy multivitamin already supplies the recommended supplement. Iodine matters for women with a functioning gland, which is the distinction between prevention and replacement. (Source: NHMRC: Iodine Supplementation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: NHMRC: Iodine Supplementation in Pregnancy

options.text: Switch to liothyronine 20 micrograms daily to provide the active hormone directly to the foetus
options.rationale: Liothyronine is avoided in pregnancy because triiodothyronine crosses the placenta poorly while thyroxine crosses adequately, so the foetal brain would be deprived of substrate. The near pair reasoning that the active hormone must be better is exactly what fails here, because placental transfer rather than potency is the constraint. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Continue the current dose and check thyroid function at the routine 12 week antenatal visit
options.rationale: Waiting until 12 weeks leaves the first trimester uncovered, which is the very period when the foetus depends entirely on maternal thyroxine because its own gland is not yet functioning. Her pre-pregnancy result being normal is reassurance about the non pregnant state only. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Increase the dose by about 25 to 30 per cent now and check thyroid function within two weeks
options.rationale: Thyroxine requirements rise by roughly a quarter to a third in early pregnancy because of increased thyroxine binding globulin, the thyrotropic effect of human chorionic gonadotrophin and a larger distribution volume, and the increase is made as soon as pregnancy is confirmed rather than after a test. A practical way to achieve this is to add two extra daily doses each week, and the level is then rechecked within a fortnight and every four weeks through the first half of pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy
American Thyroid Association: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Reduce the dose by about 25 per cent now to avoid foetal thyrotoxicosis in the first trimester
options.rationale: Requirements rise rather than fall in pregnancy, and maternal thyroxine at replacement doses does not cause foetal thyrotoxicosis, which is instead driven by transplacental passage of stimulating antibodies in Graves disease. Reducing the dose would produce exactly the maternal hypothyroidism that harms neurodevelopment. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Maternal thyroxine is the sole source of thyroid hormone for the foetus until the foetal gland begins producing at around 12 to 16 weeks, so untreated or undertreated maternal hypothyroidism in the first trimester is linked with miscarriage, preterm birth and reduced childhood cognitive scores. The physiological demand rises sharply and early, driven by oestrogen induced increases in thyroxine binding globulin, weak thyroid stimulating hormone receptor activity of human chorionic gonadotrophin, and placental deiodinase activity. Because of the lag between changing a dose and seeing the effect, the increase is made empirically at the time of the positive test rather than waiting for a level to drift. Trimester specific targets are used, with most services aiming for a thyroid stimulating hormone below 2.5 mIU/L in the first trimester. Women planning pregnancy should ideally be optimised before conception, and any woman on thyroxine should be told in advance what to do the day she tests positive.
key_points: Thyroxine requirement rises about 25 to 30 per cent, beginning in the first weeks of pregnancy.
Make the increase when pregnancy is confirmed, not after a repeat level has come back.
An easy practical instruction is to take two additional daily doses each week.
Recheck thyroid function within two weeks and then roughly every four weeks until mid pregnancy.
Separate thyroxine from iron and calcium containing supplements by at least four hours.
explanation.pearls: The pregnancy multivitamin itself can be the cause of a rising thyroid stimulating hormone, because the iron and calcium it contains bind thyroxine in the gut, so ask when the two tablets are taken before assuming the dose is inadequate.

sources.label: American Thyroid Association: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: timing maternal pertussis immunisation to maximise transplacental antibody transfer in a woman vaccinated in a recent previous pregnancy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar running an antenatal visit for a 29-year-old woman at 21 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first child is 18 months old and is fully immunised.

She tells you she had a whooping cough vaccine at 30 weeks in her previous pregnancy and does not think she needs another one so soon, since her father was told an adult booster lasts ten years. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated, her morphology scan yesterday was normal, and her blood pressure and urinalysis today are unremarkable. She had an influenza vaccine three weeks ago without any reaction. She has no history of Guillain Barre syndrome, no allergy to vaccine components and no immunosuppression.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height consistent with dates, foetal movements reported as normal
data_table.Investigations: Morphology scan at 20 weeks reported as normal, urinalysis negative
data_table.Immunisation history: Pertussis containing vaccine at 30 weeks of previous pregnancy 18 months ago, influenza vaccine 3 weeks ago

lead_in: What would you recommend regarding pertussis immunisation in this pregnancy?

options.text: Defer the vaccine until 34 to 36 weeks so that antibody levels peak closest to the birth
options.rationale: Vaccinating this late reduces the time available for antibody to be actively transported across the placenta, which is the step that protects the newborn, and cord levels are highest when the dose falls in the 20 to 32 week window. The near pair error is reasoning about the mother's peak titre when what matters is the infant's cord titre. (Source: NCIRS: Maternal Pertussis Vaccination)
source_refs: NCIRS: Maternal Pertussis Vaccination

options.text: Defer the vaccine until immediately after birth, before she is discharged from hospital
options.rationale: Postpartum vaccination protects the mother from becoming a source of infection but transfers nothing to the baby, leaving the newborn unprotected through the weeks when pertussis is most lethal. This cocooning approach is the fallback for women who were not vaccinated antenatally. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Pertussis)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Pertussis

options.text: Omit the vaccine in this pregnancy because a dose was given less than two years ago
options.rationale: No minimum interval applies between pregnancies for this indication, and the antibody from a dose 18 months ago has already declined well below the level that protects a newborn. Repeat dosing in successive pregnancies has been shown to be safe. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Pertussis)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Pertussis

options.text: Check her pertussis serology now and vaccinate only if the antibody titre is found to be low
options.rationale: There is no serological correlate of protection for pertussis that can be used to make an individual vaccination decision, so a titre cannot identify who needs a dose. Testing would add cost and delay to a decision that is made on the recommendation itself. (Source: NCIRS: Maternal Pertussis Vaccination)
source_refs: NCIRS: Maternal Pertussis Vaccination

options.text: Give a pertussis containing vaccine now, since it is recommended in every pregnancy
options.rationale: A pertussis containing vaccine is recommended in every pregnancy regardless of the interval since the last dose, because the protective antibody transferred across the placenta is generated by that pregnancy's own dose and wanes within about a year. The optimal window is 20 to 32 weeks, and at 21 weeks she sits at the start of it. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Pertussis)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Pertussis
NCIRS: Maternal Pertussis Vaccination

explanation.summary: Pertussis causes its greatest harm in infants under six months, who are too young to have completed their own primary course, and maternal immunisation exists specifically to bridge that gap by delivering antibody across the placenta before birth. Active transplacental transport of immunoglobulin G accelerates through the third trimester, so a dose given in the second half of pregnancy produces high cord blood levels while a very late dose leaves insufficient time. The Australian recommendation is a dose in every pregnancy between 20 and 32 weeks, funded under the National Immunisation Program, with vaccination still worthwhile up to delivery if the window is missed. The vaccine used is the reduced antigen adult formulation combined with diphtheria and tetanus, and it can be co-administered with influenza vaccine. Household contacts who have not had a booster in the previous ten years should also be offered one.
key_points: Recommend a pertussis containing vaccine in every pregnancy, with no minimum interval between pregnancies.
The optimal window is 20 to 32 weeks, driven by transplacental antibody transfer rather than maternal peak.
A dose is still offered after 32 weeks if the window was missed, and remains worthwhile up to delivery.
Postpartum vaccination protects the mother but delivers no antibody to the newborn.
Infant doses are due at 6 weeks, 4 months and 6 months, so maternal antibody covers the interval before completion.
explanation.pearls: Maternal vaccination in the 20 to 32 week window prevents roughly 90 per cent of pertussis cases in infants under three months, which is a larger effect than vaccinating every household contact around the baby.

subtopic_detail: deciding dose and the need for quantification of feto-maternal haemorrhage after a third trimester sensitising event in a rhesus negative woman
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite assessment area. A 27-year-old woman at 31 weeks in her first pregnancy has come in after a low speed car accident in which her abdomen struck the seatbelt. She reports no bleeding and no loss of fluid.

Her blood group is O negative and her antibody screen at 28 weeks was negative. She received her routine prophylactic anti-D at 28 weeks, six weeks before this presentation. The cardiotocograph has been reactive for 40 minutes with a baseline of 140 beats per minute, moderate variability and no decelerations, and she has had no contractions on the tocograph. Her abdomen is soft and non tender with no uterine irritability, and a bedside ultrasound shows a normally sited posterior placenta with no retroplacental collection.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 78, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 140
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no uterine activity palpable, no vaginal bleeding or liquor on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O negative, antibody screen negative at 28 weeks, full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging and monitoring: Cardiotocograph reactive for 40 minutes with no decelerations; ultrasound shows posterior placenta with no retroplacental collection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rhesus status?

options.text: Give anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscularly and send a sample to quantify foetal cells
options.rationale: Abdominal trauma after 12 weeks is a sensitising event requiring 625 IU of anti-D within 72 hours, and the routine 28 week dose does not cover a subsequent event. After 20 weeks a quantification test such as flow cytometry or a Kleihauer is also required, because a large feto-maternal bleed needs additional anti-D beyond the standard dose. (Source: ANZSBT and NBA: Guidelines for Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: ANZSBT and NBA: Guidelines for Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin
RANZCOG: Rh D Immunoglobulin in Obstetrics

options.text: Give anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscularly and repeat the antibody screen in four weeks
options.rationale: The 250 IU dose is used for sensitising events in the first trimester, when foetal red cell volume is small, and it is inadequate for a third trimester event. The near pair distinction is gestation, with 12 weeks the threshold at which the dose changes. (Source: ANZSBT and NBA: Guidelines for Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: ANZSBT and NBA: Guidelines for Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti-D because the routine 28 week prophylactic dose still provides adequate cover
options.rationale: Routine prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks covers silent feto-maternal transfusion, not a discrete sensitising event, and antibody from the earlier dose has already declined substantially by six weeks. A separate dose is required for every sensitising event whenever it occurs. (Source: RANZCOG: Rh D Immunoglobulin in Obstetrics)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Rh D Immunoglobulin in Obstetrics

options.text: Withhold anti-D because there is no vaginal bleeding and the cardiotocograph is reactive
options.rationale: Feto-maternal haemorrhage after trauma is frequently occult, with no external bleeding and a normal trace, so neither finding excludes the transfer of foetal cells. Waiting for visible blood is the reasoning error that produces preventable alloimmunisation. (Source: RANZCOG: Rh D Immunoglobulin in Obstetrics)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Rh D Immunoglobulin in Obstetrics

options.text: Send a quantification sample first and give anti-D only if foetal cells are detected in maternal blood
options.rationale: Anti-D works by clearing foetal cells before an immune response is mounted, so it is given immediately and the quantification result is used to decide whether more is needed rather than whether any is needed. Waiting for the laboratory can push administration beyond the 72 hour window in which prophylaxis is most effective. (Source: ANZSBT and NBA: Guidelines for Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: ANZSBT and NBA: Guidelines for Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Rhesus D alloimmunisation occurs when foetal D positive red cells enter the circulation of a D negative woman and provoke an antibody response that in a subsequent pregnancy crosses the placenta and destroys foetal red cells. Prophylaxis has two limbs in Australian practice: routine antenatal doses at 28 and 34 weeks to cover subclinical transfer, and an event driven dose for every sensitising episode. Sensitising events include miscarriage, termination, ectopic pregnancy, chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis, external cephalic version, antepartum haemorrhage, abdominal trauma and birth itself. The dose is 250 IU before 12 weeks and 625 IU from 12 weeks onward, given as soon as possible and always within 72 hours. From 20 weeks, quantification of feto-maternal haemorrhage is added so that additional anti-D can be given if the bleed exceeds what the standard dose can neutralise.
key_points: Anti-D dose is 250 IU before 12 weeks gestation and 625 IU from 12 weeks onwards.
Give within 72 hours of the sensitising event, and still give it late rather than not at all.
Routine 28 and 34 week doses do not substitute for an event driven dose.
From 20 weeks, quantify feto-maternal haemorrhage by flow cytometry or Kleihauer to determine whether more is needed.
Cordocentesis, external cephalic version and abdominal trauma all count as sensitising events.
explanation.pearls: A standard 625 IU dose neutralises about 6 mL of foetal red cells, roughly 12 mL of whole blood, so a quantification result above that threshold requires additional anti-D calculated on the measured volume rather than a second standard dose.

sources.label: ANZSBT and NBA: Guidelines for Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin
RANZCOG: Rh D Immunoglobulin in Obstetrics

subtopic_detail: applying the missed pill rules when two combined oral contraceptive tablets are omitted in the first week of a new packet
stem:
You are the general practice registrar taking a Monday morning telephone consultation from a 22-year-old woman who takes a combined oral contraceptive containing ethinyloestradiol 30 micrograms with levonorgestrel 150 micrograms.

She started a new packet last Wednesday after her usual hormone free interval. She took Wednesday's tablet, then went away for the weekend and forgot the packet, missing both Thursday's and Friday's tablets. She restarted on Saturday morning and has taken Saturday, Sunday and today's tablets on time. She had unprotected sex on Friday night and again on Sunday night. She is not using condoms, has no vomiting or diarrhoea, and takes no other medicines including no over the counter or herbal preparations. Her last menstrual period was the withdrawal bleed that finished last Tuesday.

data_table.Pill details: Ethinyloestradiol 30 micrograms with levonorgestrel 150 micrograms, monophasic 21 day formulation
data_table.Missed doses: Tablets 2 and 3 of the packet missed on Thursday and Friday, tablets 4 to 6 taken on time Saturday to Monday
data_table.Exposures: Unprotected intercourse Friday night and Sunday night
data_table.Other factors: No vomiting or diarrhoea, no interacting medicines, withdrawal bleed completed last Tuesday

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice to give her now?

options.text: Arrange a urine pregnancy test today and base any further contraceptive advice on that result
options.rationale: A test taken three days after the earlier exposure cannot detect an implantation that has not yet occurred, so a negative result would give false reassurance and delay emergency contraception past its most effective window. Testing has a role later, if the expected withdrawal bleed does not arrive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Offer emergency contraception, continue the packet, and use condoms for the next seven days
options.rationale: Missing two or more tablets in the first week, with unprotected intercourse in the preceding days, is the specific situation in which emergency contraception is indicated because the hormone free interval has effectively been extended and follicular development may have resumed. She continues the current packet and adds barrier cover until seven consecutive tablets have been taken. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Missed Pill Guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Missed Pill Guidance
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Continue the packet as normal and use condoms for seven days without emergency contraception
options.rationale: This is the correct advice when two or more tablets are missed in the second or third week, where the preceding weeks of consistent use have suppressed the ovary. The near pair distinction is which week of the packet the omission falls in, because week one adjoins the hormone free interval and week three does not. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Missed Pill Guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Missed Pill Guidance

options.text: Stop the current packet, omit the hormone free interval, and start a fresh packet tomorrow
options.rationale: Discarding a partly used packet restarts the seven day window for suppression from scratch and offers no advantage over continuing, while leaving the exposures already incurred untreated. Skipping the hormone free interval is a strategy for the end of a packet, not the beginning. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Missed Pill Guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Missed Pill Guidance

options.text: Take two tablets today to make up the missed doses and continue the packet as scheduled
options.rationale: Doubling up does not retrospectively restore suppression and increases nausea, and in any case she has already taken three consecutive tablets since restarting. The general instruction is to take the most recent missed tablet only and then continue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

explanation.summary: The combined oral contraceptive works principally by suppressing the mid cycle luteinising hormone surge, and that suppression depends on seven consecutive days of active tablets. The hormone free interval is therefore the vulnerable point of the cycle, and tablets missed in the first week effectively lengthen that interval and allow a follicle to escape. The standard rules distinguish one missed tablet, which requires no additional measures, from two or more, which requires seven days of additional precautions and, in week one with recent unprotected intercourse, emergency contraception as well. Omissions in week three are handled by running the packets together and skipping the hormone free interval. The same principles underlie advice about severe vomiting, diarrhoea within a few hours of a dose, and enzyme inducing medicines, all of which reduce absorbed hormone.
key_points: Seven consecutive active tablets are required to establish or restore ovulation suppression.
One missed tablet needs no additional precautions; take it as soon as remembered and continue.
Two or more missed in week one with recent unprotected sex is the trigger for emergency contraception.
Two or more missed in week three is managed by omitting the hormone free interval and starting the next packet.
Vomiting within two hours or severe diarrhoea is treated as a missed tablet.
explanation.pearls: Ulipristal acetate outperforms levonorgestrel closer to ovulation but is blocked by progestogen, so a woman who resumes her combined pill straight after taking it loses much of its effect and needs barrier cover for five days before restarting.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Missed Pill Guidance
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

subtopic_detail: choosing between oral and parenteral iron replacement in the third trimester when oral therapy has already been tried
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in an antenatal clinic reviewing a 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her third pregnancy. Her 28 week bloods showed a haemoglobin of 92 g/L (115 to 155) with a ferritin of 6 micrograms/L (30 to 200) and normal B12 and folate.

She was started on oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily eight weeks ago at her 22 week visit. She says she stopped taking it after ten days because it made her constipated and gave her stomach cramps, and she has taken nothing since. She feels tired climbing stairs but has no palpitations, chest pain or breathlessness at rest. She has no history of inflammatory bowel disease, no overt bleeding, and no known allergy. Her booking haemoglobin at 11 weeks was 118 g/L and her previous two pregnancies were uncomplicated with vaginal births.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 88, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 142
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, fundal height consistent with dates, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 6 micrograms/L (30 to 200), mean cell volume 74 fL (80 to 100), B12 and folate within normal limits
data_table.Treatment history: Ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily commenced at 22 weeks, self ceased after 10 days for gastrointestinal side effects

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her anaemia?

options.text: Prescribe an oral iron polymaltose preparation and review the full blood count at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Changing the oral salt can reduce gastrointestinal intolerance and is reasonable earlier in pregnancy, but polymaltose is absorbed more slowly than the ferrous salts and reviewing only at 36 weeks leaves no time to change course. This chooses tolerability at the cost of the timeline. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Iron)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Iron

options.text: Investigate for a gastrointestinal source of blood loss with faecal occult blood and coeliac serology
options.rationale: Pregnancy itself explains iron deficiency through an expanded red cell mass and foetal demand, and she has no overt bleeding, no family history and two previous uncomplicated pregnancies. Pursuing a gastrointestinal source now would delay treatment that is needed before birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange an intravenous iron infusion with ferric carboxymaltose in the day assessment unit
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is indicated when oral iron has been tried and not tolerated, when absorption is impaired, or when the gestation is too advanced for oral repletion to work in time, and at 30 weeks with a ferritin of 6 micrograms/L all three considerations point the same way. Parenteral iron can be given from the second trimester onwards and raises haemoglobin substantially faster than oral therapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy
Australian Medicines Handbook: Iron

options.text: Restart oral ferrous sulfate at the same dose taken on alternate days with vitamin C
options.rationale: Alternate day dosing genuinely improves absorption by reducing the hepcidin surge and is a sound strategy earlier in pregnancy, but it still takes months to replete stores and she has ten weeks left. The near pair distinction is time available rather than efficacy of the regimen. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells and recheck the full blood count the following day
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, active bleeding or imminent birth with severe anaemia, and it carries alloimmunisation and transfusion reaction risks with no benefit to iron stores. She is stable at rest and has ten weeks in which iron can be replaced properly. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management Guidelines, Obstetrics)
source_refs: NBA: Patient Blood Management Guidelines, Obstetrics

explanation.summary: Iron requirements roughly triple across pregnancy as maternal red cell mass expands and the foetus accumulates iron, mostly in the third trimester, so deficiency is the commonest medical problem of pregnancy in Australia. Ferritin is the most useful single test, with values below 30 micrograms per litre indicating depleted stores even when the haemoglobin is still normal, although it rises as an acute phase reactant and can mislead during infection. Oral iron remains first line and works well when started early and tolerated, with alternate day dosing improving absorption and reducing side effects. Intravenous iron is reserved for intolerance, malabsorption, non response, or a gestation too advanced for oral repletion, and modern preparations allow total dose replacement in a single sitting. Correcting anaemia before birth matters because it reduces the chance that a postpartum haemorrhage of ordinary size becomes a transfusion event.
key_points: Ferritin below 30 micrograms per litre indicates depleted iron stores regardless of the haemoglobin.
Oral iron taken on alternate days is absorbed better than daily dosing because of hepcidin kinetics.
Intravenous iron is appropriate from the second trimester for intolerance, malabsorption or late gestation.
Transfusion is for haemodynamic compromise or active bleeding, not for a number alone.
Correcting antenatal anaemia lowers the transfusion risk if postpartum haemorrhage occurs.
explanation.pearls: Ferric carboxymaltose causes hypophosphataemia in a substantial minority through increased fibroblast growth factor 23 activity, so persistent fatigue or bone pain weeks after an infusion warrants a serum phosphate rather than a repeat iron study.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy
NBA: Patient Blood Management Guidelines, Obstetrics

subtopic_detail: selecting first line management of symptomatic anterior compartment prolapse in a woman who has not completed her family
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in an outpatient clinic seeing a 34-year-old woman who describes a dragging sensation and a feeling of something coming down at the vaginal entrance, worse by the end of a working day and relieved by lying flat.

She had a forceps birth eighteen months ago with a second degree tear and has a 4-year-old from a previous normal birth. She and her partner would like one more child and are not using contraception. She has no urinary incontinence, empties her bladder and bowel completely, and has no pain with intercourse. On examination with Valsalva in the semi-recumbent position, the anterior vaginal wall descends to 1 cm above the hymen with no descent of the cervix or posterior wall. She has palpable voluntary pelvic floor contraction with a Modified Oxford score of 2 out of 5 and holds it for two seconds.

data_table.Examination: Anterior vaginal wall descends to 1 cm above the hymen on Valsalva; cervix and posterior wall show no descent; Modified Oxford score 2 out of 5 with a 2 second hold
data_table.Symptoms: Dragging sensation worse at the end of the day, relieved by lying flat; no urinary or faecal incontinence; no incomplete emptying; no dyspareunia
data_table.Obstetric history: Forceps birth 18 months ago with second degree tear, previous normal birth, planning a further pregnancy

lead_in: What would you recommend as first line management?

options.text: Refer for anterior colporrhaphy with a plan to deliver any future pregnancy by caesarean
options.rationale: Reconstructive surgery before a planned pregnancy is generally avoided because a subsequent pregnancy and birth compromises the repair, and recurrence rates after anterior repair are already substantial. Planning a caesarean to protect the repair commits her to abdominal birth for an operation she may not yet need. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse

options.text: Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen cream three nights per week and review in three months
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen improves atrophic tissue quality and is a useful adjunct around pessary use or surgery in postmenopausal women, but she is premenopausal with normally oestrogenised tissue. It treats a tissue problem she does not have. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse

options.text: Arrange urodynamic studies to characterise bladder function before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Urodynamics is indicated where there is bothersome incontinence, suspected voiding dysfunction, or before surgery for a complex case, and she has neither incontinence nor incomplete emptying. Investigating first would delay a treatment that is safe to start on clinical grounds alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse

options.text: Refer for supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a pelvic health physiotherapist
options.rationale: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is first line for symptomatic prolapse at or above the hymen and improves both symptoms and stage, and her weak but present voluntary contraction is exactly the substrate that responds to a structured programme. It is also the option that does not commit her to anything before a planned further pregnancy, which would undo a surgical repair. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse
Cochrane: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training for Prolapse

options.text: Fit a ring pessary in clinic today and arrange a review appointment in three months
options.rationale: A pessary is a reasonable conservative option and is the usual choice when symptoms are severe, when training has failed, or when surgery is not wanted, but it is second line for mild prolapse with an intact voluntary contraction. The near pair distinction is that a pessary supports the prolapse mechanically whereas training addresses the muscle deficit causing it. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse

explanation.summary: Pelvic organ prolapse is graded by the position of the leading edge relative to the hymen, and symptoms correlate poorly with stage until the prolapse reaches or passes that landmark. Vaginal birth, particularly instrumental birth, is the dominant risk factor, alongside increasing parity, obesity, chronic cough and constipation, and prolonged heavy lifting. Management follows a ladder from lifestyle and pelvic floor muscle training, through mechanical support with a pessary, to reconstructive or obliterative surgery. Supervised training delivered by a pelvic health physiotherapist is substantially more effective than a leaflet of instructions, and trials show benefit for both symptoms and objective stage in mild to moderate disease. Surgical repair is deferred where further childbearing is planned, since a subsequent birth commonly undoes it.
key_points: Stage is defined by the leading edge relative to the hymen, with symptoms becoming prominent at or beyond it.
Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is first line for mild to moderate symptomatic prolapse.
A pessary is the next step for those who do not improve, or who prefer to avoid or defer surgery.
Reconstructive surgery is generally deferred until childbearing is complete.
Address constipation, chronic cough and heavy lifting as modifiable contributors in every case.
explanation.pearls: Around a third of women cannot perform a correct pelvic floor contraction from verbal instruction alone and instead bear down, which is why a digital assessment confirming a lift rather than a push should precede any home exercise programme.

sources.label: Cochrane: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training for Prolapse
